claims.text: An ADR should list the options the team seriously considered, keeping things as they are among them, and judge each against the same needs, so a reader can check the choice.
claims.source_hint: Outline item 1; examples/don-hang @ stage-3 docs/adr/template.md lines 13-19

claims.text: Đơn Hàng's docs/adr/template.md options section asks for each option the team really considered, including keeping things as they are, weighed against the same needs from the context section, each with what it gains and loses.

ADR 0003's context: YC-7 accept a refund request within 2 s even if the gateway fails, YC-9 never refund twice, YC-10 resend within 24 h; the gateway's API key and the money rows are the most sensitive part; in version 1 every DonHang.Api copy holds the key and can read/write payments.

ADR 0003 lines 19-28 weigh: refunds in DonHang.Api as version 1 of refund-design.md (gain one transaction; cost key and money rows in the biggest service), a Payments service joined by a saga (gain only: key and money in one service), and two-phase commit (neither stated).

ADR 0003 lines 32-36 choose the saga; reject 2PC as the gateway's HTTP API has no prepare step and RabbitMQ takes no part in a PostgreSQL transaction; reject the in-API option as key and money rows would not sit in a service of their own. No rejection cites YC-7, YC-9 or YC-10.

ADR 0003's consequences include that the order and the refund agree only after a while (order at refunding while the Payments row is pending) and one more service to run with its database, image and dashboard.

Arrows from the needs mean each option was proposed to meet them, not scored against each; two-phase commit is rejected on whether it can be built at all, the in-API option on the key-and-money need; the 0004 read model keeps how Order is stored though it adds a table.
claims.source_hint: Reading of docs/adr/0003 @ stage-3 lines 32-36 against lines 11-17; docs/adr/0004 lines 21-22

claims.text: Listing the chosen option's costs in the consequences keeps readers from taking the decision as free; with the same needs and options written down, a later reader can redo the comparison and see whether each reason still holds.

ADR 0004 lines 18-23 list three options: event sourcing for Order, keeping Order state-based with an order_status_history read model updated from domain events in the same transaction, and reading outbox_messages.

ADR 0004 lines 27-29 decide not to event-source Order because the need is one list per order while event sourcing changes how every use case, query and test loads and saves an order; the ADR gives no reason of its own against reading outbox_messages.
ADR 0004 lines 9-10 point to docs/design/order-history-design.md for the three options and how they were compared; that design doc explains why reading outbox_messages lost (Phương án C).
claims.source_hint: docs/adr/0004 @ stage-3 lines 9-10; docs/design/order-history-design.md @ stage-3, Phương án C

claims.text: ADR 0004 consequences (lines 33-34): orders from before stage-3 have only a placed row in their history, and each status change adds one INSERT.

ADR 0004 lines 36-38 name three reasons to revisit: a requirement to show the whole order at any past moment, many new read models needing the order's changes, or an audit demanding proof the history was never edited.
Rejected options written down let a reader check a choice and keep a rejected idea from being proposed again as new without a fresh discussion.
An ADR that hides its chosen option's costs reads as a promise the system cannot keep; a known cost left out tends to be reported later as a bug or met first in operations.
Keeping things as they are has costs too and is worth writing down as an option, so a reader can judge whether a change was worth its own costs.
